1394.title: B-R-A
1394.hook: bara: to create, in the Torah used only of God
1394.howItsDone: Jews begin the yearly cycle of Torah reading with Bereshit, "in the beginning," and Jewish commentators often note that the verb bara, to create, is reserved in the Torah for God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, M-Ch-L: mechilah, waiving what you're owed, a small one before sleep. Today, a new week, and the verb in the Torah's opening line.

The Torah's opening line has a subject and a verb. The subject is God. The verb is bara. Bereshit bara Elohim: in the beginning, God created. English is generous with create. People create playlists, problems, a stir at the dinner table. Hebrew has plenty of words for making and building, and people use them all the time. But this one, in the Torah, is kept for a single subject. Bet, resh, alef: B-R-A. A verb with a reserved seat.
screen: `BERESHIT BARA ELOHIM.` → `CREATE A PLAYLIST?` → `B-R-A: A RESERVED VERB.`

segments.voice: You met that opening line on day twenty-two. Now, its verb. Turn it four ways. First, the subject. Jewish commentators point out that in the Torah, bara is used only of God. People make, build, shape and plant. God creates. Second, the surprises. Bara turns up at the start, "God created the heaven and the earth," then goes quiet. When it returns, it's for something unexpected: "And God created the great sea-monsters." Not the sun or the trees, but the creatures of the deep. Some readers take that as a hint that even the things people fear most are inside creation, not outside it. Then it comes three times in one verse, for human beings. Third, the pair. On the seventh day, God rests from all His work "which God in creating had made," in the old Jewish Publication Society translation. Creating, bara. Made, asah. Some Jewish commentators read the Hebrew as created to make, and hear an unfinished world: God creates, and leaves the making to go on in human hands. Fourth, the heart. A psalm asks for this verb to happen again, inside a person: "Create me a clean heart, O God." Not fix, not repair. Create, as if some things need more than patching. So the verb at the top of the Torah returns in a prayer, as a request for something new.
screen: `THE SUBJECT: ONLY GOD CREATES.` · `THE SURPRISE: THE GREAT SEA-MONSTERS.` · `THE PAIR: CREATED, AND MADE.` · `THE HEART: CREATE ME A CLEAN HEART.` · then, large: `בָּרָא`

segments.voice: Make one small thing that wasn't here a minute ago, nothing useful and nothing anyone will grade: a line of words, a doodle in a margin, a few notes hummed in a new order, a paper fold. Don't fix it or judge it; just notice what it's like to bring one new thing into the room. If you pray, you can hold the psalm's line about a clean heart while you work.
B-R-A. Bet, resh, alef: the root of bara, to create, the verb of the Torah's opening line, which in the Torah has God as its subject. Today's word.
Your line: create. Some commentators read the world as left with making still to do. On to tomorrow.

1395.title: Y-Tz-R
1395.hook: yetzer, the impulse, and yatzar, to form, like a potter
1395.howItsDone: Jewish teaching speaks of the yetzer tov and the yetzer hara, the good and bad impulses, and Jewish ethical and Hasidic writings treat the work of a life as shaping and channeling the yetzer rather than destroying it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, B-R-A: bara, the verb the Torah keeps for God. Today, the verb for shaping what's already there.

A lump of clay sits on a wheel. The potter's hands close around it, wet, the wheel spins, and a wall begins to rise. Push too hard and it collapses. Too gently and nothing happens. Hebrew has a verb for exactly this, yatzar, to form, and a potter is a yotzer, a former. From the same root comes a word Jewish tradition uses for something inside a person: yetzer, the impulse, the urge. Yud, tzadi, resh: Y-Tz-R. Clay on the outside, and clay on the inside.
screen: `CLAY ON A WHEEL.` → `YOTZER: A POTTER.` → `Y-TZ-R: TO FORM.`

segments.voice: Turn this root four ways. First, the dust. In the second chapter of Genesis the verb changes: "Then the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life." Formed is yatzar: a potter at work, dust shaped by hand. Second, the two yuds. In Hebrew, formed, vayyitzer, is spelled with two yuds where one would do. The Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, notices, and reads them as two impulses: the yetzer tov, the good impulse, and the yetzer hara, the bad one. A person is formed with both. Third, the impulse, which you first met on day one hundred sixty-four. After the flood, the text says plainly, "the imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth." Imagination is yetzer. Yet the rabbis refuse to call it simply evil. A midrash on creation says the urge is part of what God called very good, because without it nobody would build a house, marry, or raise a family. For these rabbis, the impulse is raw material, not the enemy. Fourth, the wheel, from day eight hundred two. Jeremiah goes down to the potter's house. A vessel goes wrong in the potter's hand, and he doesn't throw out the clay. He makes it again, into another vessel. Then the word comes: "as the clay in the potter's hand, so are ye in My hand." Formed, and able to be formed again.
screen: `THE DUST: FORMED BY HAND.` · `THE TWO YUDS: TWO IMPULSES.` · `THE IMPULSE: RAW MATERIAL, NOT THE ENEMY.` · `THE WHEEL: FORMED AGAIN.` · then, large: `יָצַר`

segments.voice: Notice an urge that's around today, to check your phone, to snap at someone, to eat something, to quit, and hold it the way a potter holds clay, as material, without fighting it or obeying it yet. Ask what shape it could take: the urge to snap could become one honest sentence later, the urge to quit a real break. Let your hands rest open, as if something soft were in them.
Y-Tz-R. Yud, tzadi, resh: the root of yatzar, to form, like a potter, and of yetzer, the impulse a person is formed with. Today's word.
Your line: form. Two yuds, two impulses, one person. Back tomorrow, same hill.

what it means: yetzer is the urge a person is formed with, raw material to be shaped.

options: The rabbis say no: without the urge, nobody would build a house or marry. It's raw material.

1396.title: Ch-K-M
1396.howItsDone: In Jewish life a learned scholar is called a talmid chacham, a student of the wise, and Jews often study Pirkei Avot, including Ben Zoma's teaching on who is wise, on Shabbat afternoons in the summer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Y-Tz-R: yatzar, to form, like a potter, and yetzer, the impulse. Today, wisdom, the Hebrew way.

The person in your family who can fix anything. The aunt who knows exactly what to say at a funeral. The grandfather who rarely gives advice, but when he does, it lands. None of them may have a degree in anything. English calls them handy, or tactful, or sharp. Hebrew can use one word for all three: chochmah, wisdom. And the Torah uses it, strikingly, for a craftsman. Chet, kaf, mem: Ch-K-M. Wisdom with its sleeves rolled up.
screen: `THE ONE WHO CAN FIX ANYTHING.` → `THE ONE WHO KNOWS WHAT TO SAY.` → `CH-K-M: WISDOM.`

segments.voice: Turn this root four ways. First, the hands. When the tabernacle is built in the wilderness, God says of the craftsman Bezalel, whom you met on day three hundred sixty-four, "I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship." Wisdom lives in his hands: cutting stones, carving wood, working gold. A few chapters later, the women who spin for the tabernacle are called wise-hearted. Wisdom, in the Torah, can be a skill. Second, the beginning. Proverbs, one of the Bible's books of wisdom, sets a starting line: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom." Some readers hear fear as closer to awe: knowing you aren't the center of everything. Cleverness without awe isn't wisdom yet. Third, the learner. In Pirkei Avot, the same Ben Zoma who asked who is honored asks: who is wise? The one who learns from every person. Not the one with the most answers; the one with the most teachers. Fourth, the asking. Proverbs puts it this way: the fool is sure his own way is right, while the wise one listens to advice. Wisdom isn't only something you have. It's something you go and get, from someone else. So chochmah looks less like a trophy on a shelf and more like a craft: practiced with your hands, rooted in awe, learned from anyone, and asked for out loud.
screen: `THE HANDS: BEZALEL'S CRAFT.` · `THE BEGINNING: AWE FIRST.` · `THE LEARNER: FROM EVERY PERSON.` · `THE ASKING: THE WISE ONE LISTENS.` · then, large: `חָכְמָה`

segments.voice: Think of a question you've been carrying alone: a decision, a worry, a conversation you don't know how to start. Then think of someone whose judgment you trust, not necessarily the smartest person you know, but the one with chochmah in their hands or in how they listen, and shape the question in a sentence or two, the way you'd actually say it. If you pray, you can ask for an understanding heart first.
Ch-K-M. Chet, kaf, mem: the root of chochmah, wisdom, and chacham, a wise person. In the Torah, it can be the skill of a craftsman's hands. Today's word.
Your line: wisdom. Sometimes it lives in a pair of hands. See you tomorrow, friend.

1397.title: Tz-V-H
1397.hook: mitzvah, a command; Hasidic teachers link it to tzavta, togetherness
1397.howItsDone: Jews speak of the mitzvot as the commandments of the Torah, while in everyday speech a mitzvah often means a good deed; some Hasidic teachers connect the word to tzavta, togetherness, and describe each mitzvah as a moment of connection with God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ch-K-M: chochmah, wisdom in the hands and in the listening. Today, a word you may know from the kitchen.

"Do me a mitzvah and grab the door." In Jewish kitchens, mitzvah can mean a good deed, a kindness, a favor. Helping an old man with his groceries: a mitzvah. Showing up at a shiva house with a casserole: a mitzvah. But the word underneath is sterner. A mitzvah is a command, something you're told to do. A bar mitzvah or bat mitzvah is, word for word, a son or daughter of the commandment. So which is it, a favor or an order? Tzadi, vav, hey: Tz-V-H. And a teaching that holds both.
screen: `GRAB THE DOOR: A MITZVAH.` → `A GOOD DEED, OR A COMMAND?` → `TZ-V-H: TO COMMAND.`

segments.voice: You met mitzvah on day six; today, its root. Turn it four ways. First, the order. Tzivah means he commanded, and mitzvah is the thing commanded. In the Torah it's the language of instruction, not suggestion. Second, the distance. Near the end of Deuteronomy, Moses says: "For this commandment which I command thee this day, it is not too hard for thee, neither is it far off." And: "the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it." A command, here, isn't a weight lowered from above. It's close. Third, the link. Some Hasidic teachers heard in mitzvah an echo of the Aramaic tzavta, togetherness, joining. To them, a mitzvah is a point of connection: when a person does what God asks, the person and God are joined, for that moment, in one act. This is a teacher's play on sound, not a dictionary's history of the word. Fourth, the chain. In Pirkei Avot, Ben Azzai teaches that one mitzvah draws another after it. Do one, and the next is easier to see. Some readers see it between people too: the neighbor you helped with groceries is the neighbor you notice next week. So the kitchen and the sermon aren't far apart. A mitzvah is a command, and in the Hasidic reading, a way of being joined.
screen: `THE ORDER: MITZVAH, A COMMAND.` · `THE DISTANCE: NOT FAR OFF.` · `THE LINK: TZAVTA, TOGETHERNESS.` · `THE CHAIN: ONE DRAWS ANOTHER.` · then, large: `מִצְוָה`

segments.voice: Think of one good act that would be better done together than alone: visiting someone who's lonely, cooking for a family with a new baby, clearing a neighbor's walk, giving to a cause side by side. Choose the act and the person you'd invite, and picture the two of you doing it, noticing what the doing together adds. If you pray, you can bring both names into the quiet.
Tz-V-H. Tzadi, vav, hey: the root of mitzvah, a command, which some Hasidic teachers link to tzavta, togetherness. Today's word.
Your line: command and connection. A favor and an order can be the same word. Until next time.

1398.title: H-L-Ch
1398.hook: halakha, from the root to walk
1398.howItsDone: Halakha, Jewish law, guides daily matters from blessings over food to Shabbat and business ethics; Orthodox Jews generally hold it as binding, while Conservative, Reform and other Jewish movements relate to it in different ways.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tz-V-H: mitzvah, a command, and the Hasidic echo of tzavta, togetherness. Today, the name for Jewish law.

Say the word law and a picture arrives: a courtroom, a thick book with a stern spine, a no-parking sign. Jewish law has its own thick books, shelves of them. But its Hebrew name doesn't sound like a courtroom at all. The word is halakha, and it's usually traced to a plain, everyday verb, halach, to walk. Not a verdict. A way of going. Hey, lamed, kaf: H-L-Ch. And a question that rides along: what changes if law is something you walk?
screen: `A COURTROOM? A NO-PARKING SIGN?` → `HALACH: TO WALK.` → `H-L-CH: THE WAY OF GOING.`

segments.voice: Turn this root four ways. First, the walkers. The Bible uses this verb for a whole life. "And Enoch walked with God." Abraham is told, "walk before Me, and be thou wholehearted." A walk here isn't a stroll. It's how a person goes through the years, step after step, in someone's company. Second, the road. When Moses is worn out from judging the people alone, his father-in-law Jethro tells him to show them "the way wherein they must walk." Law, in that scene, is a road you show people, so they can find their own way along it. Third, the prophet. Micah sums up what God asks in three short phrases, and the last one uses this root: "to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God." Not to arrive. To walk. Fourth, the step. Halakha deals in small, concrete things: what to say over bread, how to light candles, when to rest, how to pay a worker on time. It can sound like a long list, but a walk is made of single steps, and nobody takes them all at once. Jews in different movements understand halakha differently. Orthodox Judaism holds it as binding, while Conservative, Reform and other movements relate to it in a range of ways. Across those differences, the name itself says something: Jewish law, in its own language, is a walk, steady and ordinary, taken one step at a time.
screen: `THE WALKERS: ENOCH AND ABRAHAM.` · `THE ROAD: THE WAY WHEREIN THEY WALK.` · `THE PROPHET: WALK HUMBLY.` · `THE STEP: ONE AT A TIME.` · then, large: `הֲלָכָה`

segments.voice: If you can, stand and take a few slow steps, in a room, a hallway, a patch of grass; if you can't, let your feet press gently into the floor, one and then the other, heel, then toe. Let one question walk with you: what's the next single step in my life that I already know is right, not the whole road, only the next step? If you pray, you can carry Micah's three phrases with you as you go.
H-L-Ch. Hey, lamed, kaf: the root of halach, to walk, and of halakha, the name for Jewish law. Today's word.
Your line: law is a walk. Halakha, from halach: a way of going. See you tomorrow.

1399.title: D-R-Sh
1399.howItsDone: Jews study midrash, the rabbis' interpretive readings of scripture, often in a beit midrash, a house of study, and a short teaching on the week's Torah portion is called a d'var Torah or a drash.

segments.voice: Yesterday, H-L-Ch: halakha, Jewish law, named for walking. Today, a root for the kind of reading that digs.

A pregnant woman feels something is wrong. The children inside her are struggling against each other, and she can't make sense of it. She says, in effect, if this is how it is, why am I? Then she does something. Genesis says: "And she went to inquire of the LORD." That woman is Rebekah, and the verb is lidrosh, to seek, to ask, to search something out. The same root gives Jewish tradition its word for a searching kind of reading: midrash. Dalet, resh, shin: D-R-Sh.
screen: `REBEKAH CAN'T MAKE SENSE OF IT.` → `SHE WENT TO INQUIRE.` → `D-R-SH: TO SEEK OUT.`

segments.voice: Turn this root four ways. First, the question. Rebekah doesn't wait for an answer to arrive. She goes looking. Darash is an active verb: you get up, you go, you ask. And she gets an answer, about two nations in her womb. Second, the call. The prophet Amos puts it briefly, dirshuni vichyu: "Seek ye Me, and live." Seeking isn't a hobby. It's how you stay alive. Third, the middle. In Leviticus, Moses looks into what happened to an offering, and the text doubles the verb: darosh darash, he diligently searched. The Talmud, in tractate Kiddushin, says these two words stand at the midpoint of the Torah's words. Some teachers love that: at the Torah's center, a man searching. Fourth, the reading. When the rabbis read scripture, they asked why a word was spelled oddly, why a story stops where it does, why one verse sits beside another. That seeking is called derash, and the collections of their readings are midrash, which you met on day thirty-eight, with Abram and the idols. A beit midrash, a house of study, is, by its root, a house of seeking. Midrash can be playful, daring, even surprising. It treats the text as deep enough to keep giving, and the reader as someone who has to go and ask. So this root draws a line from a worried woman to a study hall full of arguments, both unwilling to leave a hard question alone.
screen: `THE QUESTION: REBEKAH GOES TO ASK.` · `THE CALL: SEEK ME, AND LIVE.` · `THE MIDDLE: DAROSH DARASH.` · `THE READING: A HOUSE OF SEEKING.` · then, large: `מִדְרָשׁ`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a line you know by heart, a verse, a prayer, a lyric, something a parent used to say, and say it to yourself slowly. Ask it one question the way the rabbis would: why this word and not another, why does it start there, what's missing? Don't rush to an answer; let the question sit beside the line, and if you pray, hold Amos's call, seek, and live.
D-R-Sh. Dalet, resh, shin: the root of darash, to seek, and of midrash, the rabbis' searching way of reading. Today's word.
Your line: seek. Rebekah got up and went to ask. Until tomorrow.

1400.title: P-Sh-T
1400.howItsDone: Jewish students traditionally learn the Torah with Rashi's commentary, which aims at the plain sense, and Jewish tradition holds that a verse never departs from its peshat even when it is also read through midrash.

segments.voice: Yesterday, D-R-Sh: midrash, the reading that seeks and digs. Today, the other half of reading.

Two eggs. That's the whole line on an old recipe card, in faded ink. A clever cook could read deep things into it, about pairs, about beginnings, about fragile shells. The cake doesn't care. The card means two eggs. Jewish reading has a name for what a text simply says, before anyone gets clever: peshat, the plain sense. In modern Hebrew the same root gives pashut, simple, obvious. Pey, shin, tet: P-Sh-T. Yesterday the rabbis dug. Today they make sure the ground is still there.
screen: `TWO EGGS. JUST TWO EGGS.` → `PASHUT: SIMPLE.` → `P-SH-T: THE PLAIN SENSE.`

segments.voice: Turn this root four ways. First, the cloth. In the Bible's Hebrew, the verb from this root has to do with spreading out and stripping off. When Joseph's brothers take his coat from him, the verb is this one. Peshat is a text with nothing laid over it, in plain view. Second, the anchor. The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, sets down a short rule: a verse does not leave its plain meaning. Midrash can soar, but it can't cut the rope. Even the boldest reading has to come home to the words on the page. Third, the commentator. Rashi, a medieval commentator you've sat beside since day one hundred fifty-three, says on a verse in Genesis that he has come only for the plain sense, and for those teachings that help the words make sense. Fourth, the floor. Later Jewish teachers described levels of reading, as you saw on day eight hundred eighty-five, and peshat is the floor everything else stands on. Above it come hints, seeking and secrets. But nobody climbs without a floor. Look back over the week: creating and forming, wisdom and command, walking, seeking, and now the plain. Six days of digging into words, and the seventh says: before you dig, read what's there.
screen: `THE CLOTH: NOTHING LAID OVER IT.` · `THE ANCHOR: A VERSE KEEPS ITS PLAIN SENSE.` · `THE COMMENTATOR: RASHI'S PLAIN SENSE.` · `THE FLOOR: EVERYTHING STANDS ON IT.` · then, large: `פְּשָׁט`

segments.voice: Here is a verse from the first chapter of Genesis: "And God said: 'Let there be light.' And there was light." Say it slowly and resist every urge to explain it, no symbolism, no theory, no lesson, just what it says: someone spoke, light was. Notice what the plain words do on their own, and then let yourself rest with them.
P-Sh-T. Pey, shin, tet: the root of peshat, the plain sense of a text, and of pashut, simple. Today's word.
